title: Medicines law, prescriptions and directions
blurb: Know the legal categories of medicines and the lawful routes for giving them: prescriptions, PSDs, PGDs and the rare verbal order.
question: In a sexual health clinic with no prescriber on site, a registered nurse supplies emergency contraception to a 22-year-old who meets the clinic's written criteria. Under which legal mechanism is she acting?

teach.h: Every dose needs a lawful authority
teach.body: The RPS/RCN guidance (2019) states that medicines are administered in accordance with a prescription, a Patient Specific Direction (PSD), a Patient Group Direction (PGD) or another exemption in the Human Medicines Regulations 2012. Medicines that are not prescription-only may also be given under a locally agreed homely remedy protocol. In plain English: before you give anything, you must be able to point to the document or rule that allows it.
teach.cite: RPS/RCN Professional guidance on the administration of medicines (2019), principle 1

rows: Against a prescription from a doctor, dentist or other independent or supplementary prescriber
Registered pharmacy, by or under a pharmacist's supervision
teach.caption: PGDs provide an exemption from these sale and supply restrictions for named professionals and defined patient groups (MHRA).

rows.label: What it is
values: Prescriber's instruction for a named patient
Written direction for a defined group of patients

rows.label: Prescriber assesses the patient?
values: No; the professional follows the criteria

rows.label: Example
values: Inpatient chart; written instruction in notes

rows.label: Who may act
values: Anyone competent, per policy, incl. nursing associates
Named registered professionals, e.g. nurses, midwives, paramedics, pharmacists

teach.caption: Nursing associates are not on the list of professions who can use PGDs, so they need another authority, usually a PSD.

teach.h: What a PGD cannot be used for (MHRA)
items: Controlled drugs, except those specifically allowed under the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001.

teach.body: A PGD must state the medicine, the clinical condition, inclusion and exclusion criteria, dose and maximum dose, route and frequency, warnings, follow-up and records to keep. It is signed by a doctor (or dentist) and a pharmacist, authorised by the organisation, and each professional working under it signs it individually. Its expiry should not be more than 3 years from authorisation. If a person falls outside the criteria, refer them to a prescriber.

teach.caption: Unlicensed medicines cannot be given under a PGD.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Nurse Chloe and Zara
teach.body: Chloe works in a sexual health clinic. Zara, 22, asks for emergency hormonal contraception and no prescriber is on site. The clinic has an authorised PGD that Chloe has signed. She checks Zara meets the inclusion criteria and has no exclusions, supplies and records the medicine as the PGD requires, and gives the warnings it lists. If Zara had fallen outside the criteria, Chloe would refer her to a prescriber rather than stretch the PGD.

teach.text: PSD versus PGD: a PSD is written by a prescriber for ONE named patient they have assessed (your inpatient drug chart is a PSD). A PGD covers a GROUP of unnamed patients who meet criteria. Nursing associates can work under PSDs but not PGDs.

items: Lawful routes: prescription, PSD, PGD or a legal exemption; homely remedies for non-POMs per local protocol.
POM, P and GSL are the three legal categories.
PGDs: named registered professions (not nursing associates); no unlicensed medicines, dressings, devices or abortifacients.
Verbal orders: exceptional, never for Schedule 2 CDs, confirmed in writing ideally within 24 hours.
Off-label = licensed medicine outside its licence; unlicensed = no UK licence. Both need prescriber responsibility and explanation.

summary: You can now name the legal categories of medicines and identify the lawful authority for each dose you give. You can also tell a PSD from a PGD, handle a verbal order safely and explain off-label and unlicensed use.

A.q: Elaine bought paracetamol in a supermarket, but the pharmacy told her that her codeine needed a pharmacist. Which legal category allows paracetamol to be sold in a supermarket?
options: Pharmacy medicine (P)
Prescription only medicine (POM)
General sale list medicine (GSL)
Patient group direction medicine (PGD)
A.why: GSL medicines can be sold from a wider range of premises such as supermarkets, if pre-packed and the premises can be locked (MHRA).

whyNot.0: P medicines are sold from a registered pharmacy under a pharmacist's supervision.
whyNot.1: POMs need a prescription from an appropriate prescriber.
whyNot.3: A PGD is a mechanism for supply by named professionals, not a legal category of sale.

A.q: Jamal, a registered nursing associate in a GP practice, is asked to give influenza vaccines at a Saturday clinic. The registered nurses give theirs under a PGD. Under what authority can Jamal give the vaccine?
options: Under a patient specific direction from a prescriber
Under the same PGD as the registered nurses
Under a homely remedy protocol for the clinic
Under his own nursing associate prescribing rights for vaccines
A.why: Nursing associates are not among the professions that can work under a PGD, so of these options Jamal needs a PSD from a prescriber who has assessed each patient (MHRA; RPS/RCN 2019).

whyNot.1: Nursing associates are not an eligible profession for PGDs.
whyNot.2: Homely remedy protocols apply to non-POMs; influenza vaccine is a POM.

A.q: Which of these can be supplied under a patient group direction?
options: An unlicensed specially made liquid
Mifepristone for termination of pregnancy
A compression bandage for leg ulcers
A licensed vaccine within its licence
A.why: PGDs can cover licensed medicines used within the criteria set. MHRA lists unlicensed medicines, dressings and devices, radiopharmaceuticals and abortifacients as excluded.

whyNot.0: Unlicensed medicines cannot be supplied under a PGD.
whyNot.1: Abortifacients such as mifepristone are excluded from PGDs.
whyNot.2: Dressings, appliances and devices cannot be supplied under a PGD.

B.q: Doreen, 79, is fluid overloaded and more breathless. The registrar, scrubbed in theatre for the next 2 hours, phones the ward to add a dose of IV furosemide now. Trust policy allows verbal orders in exceptional cases. What should the nurse do?
options: Accept it per policy and ensure written confirmation, ideally within 24 hours
Refuse, and wait 2 hours for the registrar to write it up
Write the prescription on the chart herself and sign it as given
Ask a healthcare assistant to listen in and witness the call, then give the dose
B.why: Verbal orders may be used exceptionally when delay would compromise care (not for Schedule 2 CDs), under policy, with the prescriber amending the prescription as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours (RPS/RCN 20).

whyNot.1: A 2-hour delay for a breathless, overloaded patient could compromise care, which is when policy permits a verbal order.
whyNot.2: A nurse without prescribing rights cannot write a prescription; that would be prescribing, not transcribing.
whyNot.3: The safeguards are policy, read-back and prompt written confirmation, not an HCA witness.

B.q: Late at night, the out-of-hours doctor phones a hospice to increase Albert's subcutaneous diamorphine dose. The doctor cannot attend for 3 hours. What should the nurse do?
options: Accept the verbal order, as diamorphine is a palliative drug
Explain it cannot be a verbal order and seek a written prescription
Give the new dose and ask the doctor to sign it in the morning
Accept it once a second registered nurse has also heard the instruction
B.why: Verbal orders are not used for Schedule 2 controlled drugs such as diamorphine (RPS/RCN 20). The nurse should seek a written or electronic prescription and use any existing as-required prescription meanwhile.

whyNot.0: Being a palliative medicine does not change its Schedule 2 status.
whyNot.2: Giving a new CD dose without a lawful prescription is unlawful.
whyNot.3: A second listener does not make a verbal order for a Schedule 2 CD acceptable.

B.q: Martha, 58, reads the leaflet for her new medicine and finds it describes a different condition from hers. The pharmacist confirms the medicine is licensed but is being used for a different indication. What is this called?
options: Unlicensed use, so the prescriber must stop it straight away
Use under a patient group direction
A dispensing error that must be reported
Off-label use, and the prescriber should explain it to her
B.why: Using a licensed medicine outside its licence terms, such as for a different indication, is off-label use. The MHRA expects prescribers to give enough information and take responsibility.

whyNot.0: The medicine is licensed; unlicensed means no UK marketing authorisation.
whyNot.1: Martha has an individual prescription, not supply under a PGD.
whyNot.2: The pharmacist has confirmed the medicine is intended; the leaflet simply describes the licensed uses.

C.q: In a nursing home, the GP reviews Hilda, 88, by video call and decides to reduce her bisoprolol from tomorrow. The GP cannot visit to amend the chart. How should the change be communicated?
options: By the nurse amending the chart herself from her own notes of the call
By a secure electronic message from the GP, with records updated
By the nurse continuing the old dose until the GP next visits
By Hilda's daughter passing on the GP's instructions
C.why: If the prescriber cannot amend the chart, the change is communicated by an appropriately secure electronic method and the patient's records are updated (RPS/RCN 20.2).

whyNot.0: Changing a prescription from notes of a call is not a lawful or auditable route.
whyNot.2: Continuing a dose the prescriber has changed delays the intended treatment.
whyNot.3: A relative relaying instructions is not a secure or auditable prescriber communication.

C.q: A practice nurse works under a PGD for travel vaccines. A patient who falls under an exclusion in the PGD asks to be vaccinated anyway. What should she do?
options: Vaccinate, as the patient consents and understands the risk
Ask a colleague who also signed the PGD to give the dose
Vaccinate, and document why she departed from the PGD
Refer the patient to a prescriber as the PGD instructs
C.why: A PGD includes exclusion criteria and when to refer to a doctor or other prescriber. Supplying outside the PGD criteria is not covered by it.

whyNot.0: Consent does not extend the legal cover of a PGD to an excluded patient.
whyNot.1: Every professional working under the PGD is bound by the same exclusions.
whyNot.2: Documenting a departure does not make it lawful; the PGD does not cover excluded patients.

C.q: Shirley, 74, says her blood pressure tablets look different from last month's and asks if they are the wrong tablets. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Check it matches the prescription and explain generics vary
Reassure her that they look different and give them
Withhold all of her tablets until the GP has reviewed her medicines
Return the tablets to pharmacy and miss today's dose
C.why: Different generic manufacturers produce tablets of different appearance. Checking the medicine and strength against the prescription answers her concern and keeps the dose on time.

whyNot.1: Reassurance without checking misses a possible dispensing error.
whyNot.2: Withholding all medicines without a reason risks harm.
whyNot.3: Missing a dose is unnecessary when a check can resolve the question.

reteach.title: Who decided this dose was right for this person?
reteach.question: Before you give a medicine, ask: who decided it, and on what basis?

blocks.body: With a prescription or PSD, a prescriber assessed this person and decided. With a PGD, an organisation, doctor and pharmacist decided in advance for a group, and you apply their written criteria. With a homely remedy protocol, a local policy decided for a non-prescription medicine. If you cannot trace the decision back to one of these, you do not have authority to give it.

explain.body: POM: needs a prescription from an appropriate prescriber. P: sold in a registered pharmacy under a pharmacist's supervision. GSL: wider outlets, pre-packed, lockable premises.

test.q: Which legal category of medicine requires a prescription from an appropriate prescriber?
options: General sale list medicine (GSL)
Pharmacy medicine
Prescription only medicine
Homely remedy
test.why: POMs must be supplied according to a prescription from a doctor, dentist or other independent or supplementary prescriber.

whyNot.0: GSL medicines are sold without a prescription.
whyNot.1: P medicines are sold under a pharmacist's supervision without a prescription.
whyNot.3: Homely remedies are non-POMs given under a local protocol.

explain.body: An instruction from a prescriber for a medicine to be supplied or administered to a named patient after individual assessment, e.g. the inpatient chart or a written direction in the notes.

test.q: Which document is an example of a patient specific direction?
options: A trust policy for treating mild headaches
A pharmacist's list of homely remedies
A written protocol for vaccinating a whole staff group
An inpatient medicines chart written for one patient
test.why: An inpatient chart written by a prescriber for a named, assessed patient is a PSD (RPS/RCN glossary).

whyNot.0: A policy for a group of unnamed patients is not patient specific.
whyNot.1: Homely remedy lists apply to non-POMs under local protocol.
whyNot.2: A protocol for a group is a PGD-type direction, not a PSD.

explain.body: Written direction for named registered professionals to supply or administer a specified medicine to a defined group. Signed by a doctor (or dentist) and a pharmacist, authorised, and signed by each user. Expiry not more than 3 years.

test.q: What is the maximum period before a PGD should expire after authorisation?
options: 1 year
2 years
3 years
5 years
test.why: MHRA: the expiry date should not be more than 3 years from the date the PGD was authorised.

whyNot.0: 1 year may be chosen locally, but the maximum is 3 years.
whyNot.1: 2 years is within the limit but is not the maximum.

explain.body: Exceptional, only where delay would compromise care, under policy and risk assessment, not for Schedule 2 CDs, and confirmed by the prescriber ideally within 24 hours.

test.q: Within what time should a prescriber ideally confirm a verbal order in writing?
options: 1 hour
12 hours
24 hours
72 hours
test.why: RPS/RCN 20.1: the prescriber provides a prescription or amends the chart as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours.

whyNot.0: 1 hour is not the stated standard.
whyNot.1: 12 hours is not the stated standard.
whyNot.3: 72 hours is too long for an unconfirmed change.
